english_verification.review_scope: Representative current-Mod starting setup, necromancy mission gate, Beldelk event flag, selected English mission prose and formable eligibility; no exact offline English Wiki result for Black Herd, I55 or Beldelk was adopted. The existing source evidence supplies broader mission and moral claims; this pass did not repeat a whole-tree or values audit. The primary compared native idea names/descriptions with current English localisation keys (formatting codes stripped); B32 upgraded Farranean originals also use their separate flavour file. Wide source bounds are locator envelopes, not exhaustive line-by-line audits. No formal validators, tests, builds or browser checks were run.
unresolved: Offline English Wiki evidence remains OFFLINE_WIKI_NO_RESULT for Black Herd, I55 and Beldelk; no related page is promoted as a dedicated country history.
Prior official-development-diary and Reddit references are carried forward as attributed context and were not newly checked.
Historical national-idea prose and detailed mission reachability were not exhaustively audited in this translation pass.

rationale.campaign_length: 18 direct missions, with phased unlocks and events, plus four confirmed generic Centaur formable outcomes.
rationale.colonization: There is no direct mission focused on colonisation.
rationale.complexity: Projects, magic schools, advisers, battle casualties and the ruler's lifespan are interlocked.
rationale.dark_story: Necromancy, corpse-explosion magic, sacrifice and lichdom are central, not incidental.
rationale.difficulty: Critical conditions are tightly coupled, and mistakes can cost long-term magical progress; no hands-on playtest was conducted.
rationale.diplomacy: Infiltration, uniting clans and integrating Ogre mages matter, but diplomacy is not the main loop.
rationale.early_pressure: A Centaur opening, a short-lived ruler and preparation for war with the Ogres create simultaneous pressure.
rationale.magic_artifice_intensity: Two unique magical projects, necromancy and lichdom run throughout the mission tree.
rationale.narrative_density: Exile, lost knowledge, revenge, sacrifice and immortality form a continuous story.
rationale.tall_play: Magical projects and adviser preparation matter, but the endgame clearly turns toward expansion.
rationale.trade_economy: Archives, damestear and the proceeds of war support magic, but this is not a trade-focused country.
rationale.warfare: The missions call for revenge, war in the Ogre Valley and Centaur unification.

identity.appearance: A Ghanzamh Centaur clan in exile in 1444, with a distinctive opening centred on Beldelk II, lost magic and the Ogre Valley.
identity.formation_scope: I55 is a Forbidden Plains starting country. After Beldelk's event sets I55_enable_formables_flag, it can enter the generic Centaur formable branch and explicitly change to I89 Khüraen Ulaeg, J54 Altorzamh, J55 Lejdazamh or J56 Taryeanzamh.

national_ideas.scope_note: National traditions, seven national ideas and ambition only; optional idea groups and racial/government bonuses are excluded. Conditional alternatives are separate, not stacked. Accepting new ideas on formation depends on the actual event/decision and player choice.

description.text:
100 years ago, we were one of the most powerful of the Ghanzamh clans, and through that power, we nearly claimed the legacy of the Storm King. However, our clan was considered ruthless and malicious, dabbling in magical techniques considered forbidden by other centaurs… in particular, the transmutation technique known as “Markhentakruan” by which enemy corpses were rendered explosive and then detonated. It took the combined might of many of the clans of Nuzurbokh to defeat us, resulting in our exile.

Many in our former ranks attempted to find other clans that would accept them and their talents, but all rejected them due to our status as exiles or our belief in the Malula sect. We found ourselves constantly harassed by young centaurs attempting to “prove their might” against us. Such young centaurs would never find their way back to their clans, giving rise to the name that all clans now know us by: the Black Herd.

description.text:
Even as our kind were unjustly expelled from our past homeland, we did not relent. We fought, struggled and survived. It was no coincidence that after many years of struggle, we arrived in this new land. Irdaeos, god of the sky, in admiration of our endurance, perseverance, and fighting spirit, led us to its domain so that we could prosper once more.

Now, it falls to us to protect Irdaeos' domain, and show the same perseverance that we did in the past in fighting those who would seek to take our new home.

description.text:
Irdaeos’ domain, its gift to the centaurs, remains fractured. To the west, the ogres prepare their resurgence, and the humans of the Federation, emboldened by their victory against the Wild Hunt, are sure to try to push into the plains. We centaurs, however, remain divided. Only a new and strong Caehnate will be able to defend centaur-kind against these new threats.

Now, however, after the catastrophic failure of the Wild Hunt, a new opportunity arises for another clan to rise above the others, uniting Irdaeos’ domain and centaur-kind under their rule and vision.

description.text:
It is war that has most defined the identity of the plain centaurs. As a result of this, these centaurs have developed a great martial culture, with generalship considered one of the most noble professions. The greatest generals are celebrated and awarded great riches and positions of authority.

To allow these generals to signify their wealth and power to the others, a unique and ostentatious style of clothing has developed. Composed of furs of the many animals that roam the plains, these clothes are adorned with looted trinkets and the bones of hunted prey, the number of condecorations signifying the power and influence of a general.

description.text:
The Western Forbidden Plains is home to several species of megafauna, such as the Branta and the Tlalusk. The Branta is an equine herbivore, reaching a staggering ten feet in height. Characterized by its skittish nature, it often tramples upon those who scare it. The Tlalusk is a gigantic, wooly, six-legged creature almost 15 feet in height: armed with both tusks and horns, it is known for impaling those that get in its way.

With the western Centaurs’ expertise in herding, these species have slowly been domesticated and herded by ordsiwyn in the area. Both Branta and Tlalusks are highly desired by the Fathide Ogres from the west, making them an incredible product for trade. They are used not just for trade, however. These cattle are big enough to feed an ogre, let alone a Centaur, and have proven incredible draft animals, bolstering the productive capabilities of the western Centaurs beyond their brethren in the rest of the plains.

description.text: Centaurs have had a fluctuating relationship with the west ogres throughout history. The centaurs were tributaries in exchange for ogre protection and high quality ogreish iron. Even in 1444, despite negative relations with the Ogres, the iron trade’s weapons are still circulating among West Forbidden Plains centaurs, making their soldiers particularly efficient.

description.text: The Malu sect believes that the shamans are messengers of Irdaeos and that He communicates with them and blesses them with magic. The shamans hold much respect among the Malukhuga and are pillars of centaur tribal society, offering stability and mediation among the people.

description.text:
Before battlehoof or glorysong graced the plains, the world dreamed in boredom. Yet when Irdaeos enveloped her, his endless depths delivered wonders—storms, gales, nurturing rains, and his enthralling blue. Impressed, Halann took Irdaeos upon her, and, to this day, she marvels at his wild beauty.

But what of Halann’s people? While our Caehn united all of centaurkind through glorious struggle, the other mortal peoples fretted amid empty existences, unwilling to seek growth or tribulation.

By sacred ouranomancy, Irdaeos’ hues instruct us to act, felling walls, routing armies, and stampeding the weaklings who tremble before our great crimson banner. We shall become an all-consuming storm that will shatter the world, filling the sky with the ash and embers of our conquests. No bulwark, strategy, magic, wealth, nor weapon can impede the Crimson Caehnate, for those who stand against our herd’s charge will earn terminal glory before joining Halann in death.

description.text:
Those who will never glimpse Ik Magthaal mistake calm winds for peace, but as centaurs, we understand its true gravitas. Through our long history, the wind fumed like a hurricane over our failures, chilled like a blizzard to temper us, and nurtured our hindquarters with tailwinds to guide us unto tomorrow.

As the breeze quickens, we assemble, confident in its harsh lesson—calm does not mean peace. We are centaurs: chosen of Irdaeos, children of the storm, and a united people, stoic and poised to strike down against the civilized fools. With our great crimson banner stained by bloody unification, who can stand against those blessed by the wind?

description.text:
When we fled annihilation, Irdaeos honored centaurs for our strength to withstand tragedy and seek tomorrow, guiding our gallop to the vast lands of Irdülhain. However, as we raced in revelry through our new home, foes large and small, opposed to such alacritous freedom, spat litigious rebukes, set meager stone markers, and erected wooden barriers to hem our migrations. We wished to impart the glory of self-sufficient prowess, but they balked, claiming that the world stood upon lines and boundaries that could not be crossed.

These arbitrary things crafted by weak minds held us back for many generations, but our hearts eternally fumed, kindled with the primal need for emancipation. Like a storm weathers a rock face, our hooves stomped and stomped and stomped in righteous anger until their foolish notions broke.

Just as Irdaeos enveloped the world, so too shall the Crimson Caehnate stretch over Halann, for the sky honors no foolish demarcations.

name.text: The Hoofs that Shattered the Weak

description.text:
As the Crimson Caehnate, we enact vengeance upon the “civilized” who decry our virtues as “monstrous” (namely the vile three lake confederation and the elf-exalting sun worshippers), but not all of our new subjects oppose our righteous bloodthirst.

Ogres, towering behemoths, pursue a pure, ever-gnawing hunger. The hyena-like gnolls survive—neigh, thrive with thrifty tact, stripping from their subdued. Orcs, strangers we once belittled as tusked humans, swiftly bucked our expectations with their admirable might and resilience. Even the fetlock-biting goblins and kobolds, swarming within the skyless mountains, channel their anguish into cruel devices that can best a charging spearbearer. Despised and dejected, these fellow monsters marvel at our handiwork, igniting a desire for unbridled revenge.

Let us leverage their wicked impulses.

We can extol our new herdmates’ strength and viciousness, granting them part in the world-spanning carnage.

description.text:
“Scions of the fallen, did you not catch your father’s
spear glinting amid the morning rays? Has your mother’s
glorious bellow, cradled by the wind, not stroked
your hair with hope’s warmth? Mourn, for your loved
ones ran in your clan, your ordsiwyn, and now they run
in Ik Magthaal, beckoning you to revel in freedom and glory.”

– Gödacerm Wardguard comforting Wild Hunt orphans, 1445 AA

Long before we unfurled the crimson banner, our people suckled on battle’s bitter milk. We recall tales of love, dirges of mourning, and tunes of celebration, but they cloud the true lessons taught by war’s hoof-druming. We train our number to never hesitate in battle, for even the most adept fighter transforms into prey with a moment’s pause. And with each decisive victory, our warriors are reborn in body and spirit. So long as we strive to test our mettle against ourselves and our peers, we will never falter.

description.text:
Between treacherous valleys, through frozen woods, over craggy ranges, and beset by countless foes harrying us from resting, our ancestors braved horrific conditions to seek a brighter tomorrow. Our exact history before the great exodus remains shrouded (powerful seers occasionally dream of those ancestral woods we once roamed), but our oral stories recall how the gods of eternal twilight abandoned us to our fated oblivion. Despondent and adrift, our forebears could only count the rhythmic clop of their bleeding hooves until Irdaeos appeared overhead. Honoring our hardships, he blessed us with Irdülhain (Sky Home) forevermore, and centaurkind pressed on into a new era.

Much has changed since those fabled days, but as centaurs rally around the crimson banner, we declare that which Irdaeos spoke so long ago: “Weary wanderers, see now the valley over which I stretch. This vast land, I grant to you. Only by your strength and determination can you keep it within your bosom.”

description.text:
Irdülhain stretches further than any galloper’s endurance, but as the Crimson Caehante conquers ever outward, we marvel at how much further Halann stretches. Despite the daunting distances, Irdaeos’ swelling breezes and deep sky hues guide us to glory and transformation.

On our ascent, we gathered the independent and subjugated clans, ordsiwyns, and caehnates into our storm’s nexus, and, thanks to that reorganization, we united far more than just our ancestral (or even all centaur) lands. But as we increasingly roam foreign lands, the various ordsikars rumble with idleness and boredom, threatening our realm’s stability.

To divert our hurricane’s energies outward, the caehn decreed fresh lands for loyal ordsiwyn to settle. Free to pursue their own interests, these new border clans are among our most zealous warriors, and, pining for glory, many centaurs readily genuflect before the caehn of the Crimson Caehnate for the chance to trot through new territory.

description.text:
What future lies ahead of us here on the Forbidden Plains? The centaur warlords see only land to tread under their hooves, the humans mere wasteland. Only we have the wisdom to remember what these plains once were, what they can become once again: the sinew that binds the world. We will make Altorzamh the entrepot of all lands, a natural middle place between realms, an alternative to storm-driven seas and a connector of alien cultures. The towering Serpentspine was not always a wall to the world, and we must not personally grow the crop to feast upon it. Instead our country will be the connection, the bridging place.

Pound the soil flat! It is time for prosperity beyond imagining – for the Caehnate of the trader’s rug!

description.text: Do not despair! Yes, we Altor have come late to the city, to the state, and to confederation. It is tempting, perhaps, to read the latest eunuch economic analysis or Sun Elf treatise and wonder how precisely we will build such things out of whole cloth, as if this is not to our spectacular advantage. Let us be yagbaithaekh, ‘like the flowing river’ – as we etch ourselves into the earth, we will steal a little gold from it with each bend of our course. The brilliance of Rahen without its fractiousness, the tenacity of the lakes without their ponderousness, the beauty of Bulwar without its tyranny: this is the privilege of the latecomer, who may learn from another’s mistakes.

description.text:
Visiting Altorzamh, one must be forgiven for wondering where precisely the centaur warrior has disappeared to. The well-dug roads and pleasure gardens do not spill over with eager young duellists; the genteel clanmerchants and their pampered heirs have little patience even for impoliteness. For the legacy of the caehnates, look instead to the painted green roof of the gharsü: look to the post office.

A hopeful gharsüdar – a waypost-runner – joins as a child. The fastest and most tenacious of their village, they join a cohort no less rigidly drilled than the tribal ordsiwyn of old. Over more than a decade, the gharsüdar is taught to embrace death before giving up a message, to achieve astonishing feats of memory and verbal recall, and to develop a physical endurance rare even among centaurs.

Sworn to the state and to each other as sibling-runners, the gharsüdar are vital to Altorzamh’s ponderously devolved political structure, coursing along hard-pounded roads between the state’s many clanhalls. They serve as delivery runners, messengers, caravan guards and local police, and can be converted during times of war into a massive, well-oiled logistical machine.

Our cities recline at their leisure, taking up space and exuding power. After all, what is a ten mile jaunt to market for a centaur?

description.text: The harpy roost at Lorghbomar has long been a neutral interlocutor in the grand centaur drama on the plains; the wisdom and magisterial presence of their matriarchs was recognised among the clans long before the formation of Altorzamh. Any such matriarch is entitled to automatic petition in a clanhall, and their presence is warmly welcomed in the talking over of complex philosophical or political disputes. The formal archive of Altorzamh government proceedings is also kept at Lorghbomar, its location symbolising the impartiality of negotiated law.

description.text: Haulage was traditionally considered highly demeaning by our people, inviting comparison to non-sapient beasts of burden. The prestige of our postal gharsüdar has slowly eroded this stigma, however, making way for the wholesale embrace of self-drawn light artillery. While Altor cannon are thus generally on the lighter side, we can deploy in enormous numbers with a much reduced baggage train, and our nimble regiments are able to manoeuvre relatively quickly into deadly flanking positions.

description.text: A highly competitive racing format held in enormous open-air amphitheatres, the twelve athlete relay is the defining national sport of Altorzamh. An absolute phenomenon among city-dwellers, it inspires deadly local rivalries, the teams given fanciful and often pseudohistorical clan names like ‘Blood Thunder’ or ‘Wanton Eclipse’. Relay races between beloved teams attract attendees in the tens of thousands, and the scale of structure required to house so many centaurs amounts to an architectural achievement in and of itself. The most famous racers are national heroes; like the Gharsü, these races offer an echo of clan culture in a society which has largely urbanised away from it.

description.text:
In their “magnanimity” the early caehns of the Golden Tremor clan commanded the other Ordsiwyns to share “only” two-thirds of the spoils of war with the Caehnate itself. This centralisation and strict hierarchy upset many Ordsiwyn leaders and caused them to seek other ways of ensuring prosperity of their clan.

Unwilling to risk far-flung campaigns for now-taxed and thus diminished rewards, they turned their focus closer to home, beginning by guarding tribute routes, protecting their own herds, and offering paid protection to nearby villages – centaur at first, then human and ogre as well. Though the practice began out of caution and, some might say, avarice, it was not long before a significant part of the northwestern Forbidden Plains fell under the protection of one or another Ordsiwyn of Lejdazamh.

The sword still hung across a rider’s back – but it would now be drawn in defence of the flock, not in pursuit of plunder… at least most of the time.

description.text:
For most of its history, the Ogre Valley resembled a tapestry of semi-independent Fathide Ogre fiefdoms under the loose dominion of Maghargma rather than a truly united state. When the trickle of Mossmouth Ogres in the 16th century reached the Ogre Valley, it brought great discontent in the Ogre society and caused some of the northeastern Ogre lords to waver in their allegiance towards the capital.

The riders of Lejdazamh did not miss the opportunity; they swiftly seized the region and placed it under Centaur protection. Rather than despoil the settlements, Lejdazamh put them to work integrating tribute routes. The new overlords defended the turncoat ogres from Maghargma reprisals, and bound the more pragmatic chieftains through oaths of loyalty.

Yet, like all else on the Plains, these victories proved temporary. When Maghargma once again unified under a strong hand, the Caehnate – worn thin by other wars – could not hold the frontier. Nevertheless, to this day, scattered Ogre villages remain under Lejdazamh’s watch, their allegiance shaped less by kinship than by memory, trade, and the promise of a safer yoke. The border shifts like wind over the steppe: back and forth, fist against hoof, neither side ever fully surrendering what it once held.

description.text:
To destroy – that has never been beyond a Centaur’s reach. The strength of one alone is enough to break a tree; his hooves can scatter villages, topple resistance, and silence screams. But in the wake of the failed invasion of the settled peoples of the North, it became increasingly clear that strength alone could not sustain a Caehnate. If Lejdazamh was to endure, it had to do more than conquer – it had to rule.

Bringing distant Centaur clans under its yoke was a promising beginning, but it was essential to extend dominion over the settled peoples of the plains as well: humans in their wattle villages, ogres in their stone steads. These were not driven off or razed, but instead woven into the fabric of the Northern Caehnate.

Officials – often drawn from among the younger sons of Ordsiwyn leaders – were appointed as tax-collectors, gathering tribute from the settled folk. The efficiency of this system, however, rested on the premise of personal honour and culturally binding oaths – a noble foundation, but one that would prove Lejdazamh’s greatest vulnerability.

description.text:
“’Twas the ninth day of the Rain Moon – cursed be its memory – when we marched westward along the Valak into the untamed reaches of the Northern Caehnate. So came ashkosk Doshurn, proud as a springtime rooster, with no fewer than ten thousand sabres, each paired with a rifleman on foot, and a score of iron-lunged cannons dragged by sweating mules.

I drew up as part of the Third Rider Banner – moustache oiled, boots polished, sabre keen, and my pistol burnished to a mirror’s shine. We crossed the Valak to the beat of drums, and Doshurn boasted we’d be drinking booze in our new cities by summer’s end. That he was later found trampled into soup was no small irony.

The Centaurs came with first light, and our palisades swayed like drunkards. Birds scattered, and then – then came the thunder of hooves. Men fell like cut grass. Before the second line could fire, the Centaurs cast aside their pistols and drew greatswords from their backs – two-handed beasts, long and cruel, that could shear two oaks in half.

Before noon, we were fleeing down the banks of the Valak. To this day, even the bravest keep to its eastern shore, and no ashkosh has since dared plan an expedition there.”

‘Memoirs of My Life, 1659–1673,’ – Alsen Kassepp, son of Izugel

description.text:
The most peculiar custom of the centaurs of the Northern Caehnate is the Endgü, or “Oath-Kinship”. While many pastoral or martial societies have developed complex codes of honour, in the case of Lejdazamh such spoken promises has come to form the foundation of public and private life, even as Lejdazamh has assumed formal statehood.

An Endgü is formed when two individuals declare a binding oath before no fewer than three witnesses. From that moment they are joined in a sanctified bond that prioritizes the well-being of the other over personal gain. It is a curious feature of this tradition that any ambiguity in the terms of an oath must be resolved in the manner most beneficial to one’s Endgü, which has fostered not only trust but an almost competitive generosity between parties.

Though initially practiced primarily among the caehn and the Ordiswyn leaders in vertical hierarchies of governance, the ritual swiftly took root in horizontal social relations and soon enough had spread beyond the Centaur clans. These days, even human and ogre steadholders dwelling within Lejdazamh’s bounds are expected to keep their word as if they were born centaurs themselves.

description.text:
The fortresses of the sedentarised folk in the Forbidden Plains were often just stockades with high palisades, yet they proved surprisingly effective, for even a fence could present a fearsome hurdle to a creature of motion like a centaur. Since Lejdazamh’s tactics lacked siege ladders, sappers or scaling lines, static defences proved sufficient to blunt or scatter an advance of a centaur army.

Yet early defeats, especially against the Maghargma, led to innovation. Centaur warbands began targeting ogre artillery positions, overwhelming crews with their speed and capturing cannons. By 1720, a third of Lejdazamh’s artillery was seized from humans or ogres.

A new doctrine followed – open the wall, then charge. Using overlapping fire from captured guns, centaur commanders would collapse fort walls, then unleash a full advance, often with pistol volleys loosed mid-gallop, followed by sabres or greatswords drawn for the finish. One cannot help but admire the irony. The steppe-folk, long considered too wild for siegecraft and too mobile for heavy guns, came to master both in their own fashion – not by imitating the warfare of cities, but by forcing cities to fight on the plains.

description.text:
At the turn of the 19th century, the Northern Caehnate was pressed by rival centaur confederacies, harried by the expansionist Maghargma ogres and weakened from within by increasingly autonomous Ordsiwyns, yet the crisis came to a head in 1794, when the Orachav of Zabutodask launched a devastating invasion.

A large part of the territories near the lake Taeganyuul was lost and the Caehnate appeared on the verge of dissolution, its governance ceremonial at best, not being able to neither muster the riders to fend off aggression nor collect the necessary taxes to upkeep the central court. Though Lejdazamh stood on the brink of collapse, from the ashes of defeat rose caehn Rhidrin VI, and with him, his sweeping reforms.

The obsolete Gathering of Ordsiwyns was stripped of power, with former leaders challenged to traditional Nageal duels to ensure their clans’ loyalties. Rhidrin introduced fixed tax levies and mandated census-taking for the first time in the history of the Northern Caehnate. Most notably, Rhidrin codified centuries of oral custom into the Written Ordinances of 1799, a monumental effort that balanced enforceable regulation with traditional oathkeeping, overseen by judges in appointed courts and overseen by scribes.

description.text:
The Great Incursion failed.

Wild Hunt broke and shattered, was torn asunder in the aftermath of its failed invasion of the Triunic people. Seven long years did the centaurs toil under the rule of the Hunt’s Filustkhuga, just to find their "glorious death" as was desired by that sect.

The centaurs of Nuzurbokh, however, desired a different path.
Through magic they found communion with Irdaeos. The killing of their shamans by the Jolgik Uts was a major blow to their expertise, but it led to the emergence of a new prominent group of mages: the Tempestcallers.

Mastering the elements of wind and lightning, against which the Nuzurbokh centaurs had ever struggled in their storm-lashed homeland beside Zernuuk Lake, these Tempestcallers proved able to avert the worst natural disasters and channel the storm for their own purposes.
Such specialised priests, part of the Malukhuga sect, were few and far between the years after the invasion of 1433, but their fervor would propel their numbers in the years to follow.

description.text:
While historical documents regarding centaur society in Nuzurbokh in the years following the Great Incursion are rare and mostly written by Triunic mercenaries, it does seem rather clear that a significant restructuring of daily life occurred. Archeological findings show us that there were more frequent offerings to local rocs in Nuzurbokh, compared to the more western steppes, a sign of greater devotion towards Irdaeos’ messengers. Crude etchings in funeral grounds became common and much more elaborate as well during this timeframe. They all mentioned one thing: Ik Magthaal, a paradise of sorts.

Although other sects do acknowledge such a place’s existence and strive to access it, it is the Malukhuga who formed a formal Conclave of Shamans, whose purpose it was to debate and ponder the nature of this “paradise”.

description.text:
The Storm King was a well known topic of debate amongst both the shamans and those who wanted to claim his mantle, for after the passage of four centuries, even his name was lost. It was unknown which parts of his biography were true and which were myth.
But in the late 15th century, increasing trade relations with the Rukunai and Rünsukhi peoples to the east led to the discovery of written records of the Storm King, albeit from an enemy perspective.
It was surprising to see that all Rukunai accounts shared one key detail, however. The Storm King was, according to them, embraced by the Stormbringer, a roc rumored to have unbound mastery over the element of lightning. It was said that whoever this mythical creature deigned to channel its power into would share its mastery over lightning, as well as the ability to take on its form, transforming into a roc themselves. This idea of becoming chosen by the Stormbringer would serve as the bedrock of Taryeani national mythology.

A nearly region-wide search for the beast had begun.

Those documents are, of course, heavily sensationalized. All the documents pertaining to this entity were created by the Rukunai, a people this centaur has not interacted much at all with. So they can hardly be called accurate.
Eastern centaur society in the 16th century was enraptured by this Stormbringer however. So much so that the tribes of the Ghanzamh and Sochar united into a singular political entity under the second Storm King, with easternmost parts of the Teaghud centaurs chiming in.
(Though Triunic colonization efforts and the fear of being displaced certainly played a part in it)
Plans were drafted to return to Khashaalg, to slay the face stealers at last.
We do not know the name of the “second Storm King” that the caehns of Nuzurbokh rallied under, as they believed that names of Storm Kings must be struck from the record for all of time. We do know that it was a powerful Tempestcaller.
He might have found the roc, or maybe the roc found him.
We understand him as a Malukhuga shaman that created the state that we know today as Taryeanzamh - “Thunderland”.

description.text:
Centaur music was, historically speaking, usually dismissed by foreigners; Cannorians sneered at its lack of sophistication, Bulwari Elves dismissed it as sad, while the average hobgoblin found it profoundly boring.
It mostly consisted of throat singing and the percussive thundering of hooves. The instruments that they did have were made from the animals herded in the steppes and were used rather sparsely.

As the newly-founded state of Taryeanzamh consolidated and became able to enforce its borders, trade also began to flourish. The fact that their neighbors nearly universally mistrusted an actual centaur state could not prevent this.
Suddenly opened to the world, Taryeani music changed, twisted, shifted through multiple iterations remarkably quickly. One might expect that a state guided by a religious sect wishing to spread its faith beyond its borders would crack down on such a development, but there was not a reaction like this.
Instead, this transformation was welcomed, embraced even.

description.text:
Change came not only to their music.

The Centaur’s Glyphs have been a cultural tradition for eons, massive patterns etched and carved into the sands of the steppe whose purpose it is to bring glory to their god. Created not by some massive centralized effort, but by a local “ordsywin” - clan leader - such glyphs are perhaps the defining image of centaur culture to outsiders. However, with the establishment of the Conclave of Tempestcallers in 1602 - a successor of the Conclave of Shamans - this task became increasingly relegated to specialised mages.
An official division was soon thereafter sent to Remollgeibar, in order to study the greatest geoglyphs in the plains - the Glyphs of Irdaeos - which seemingly had magical properties. Their toil paid off. Standardised glyphs enchanted with one of the four primordial elements soon became an expert craft of the Taryeani Tempestcallers.
Such glyphs protected Taryeani settlements from natural disasters: droughts, floods and disastrous thunderstorms became a thing of the past.

A rotary system of permanent settlements with temporary people was soon thereafter established. Irdaeos’ domain on earth would be filled with praise for him; the Malukhuga and the second Storm King would make sure of it.

description.text:
The Triunics were the only people who refused outright to trade with the burgeoning Taryeani state, in stark contrast to the Soulseeker Ogres, Khantaar peoples, or the Siadunan Harpies.
Triunic intentions were clear: they would conquer the steppes, their long abandoned, ancestral homeland carved out from the centaurs' bullet-ridden bodies. The colonization of Nuzurbokh drove those Sochar Centaurs that did not align with Taryeanzamh out, sending them fleeing through Kashaalg and further east.

The rest of Taryeanzamh decided to resist.
Massive Tower shields were built for the strongest centaur warriors. Bows were strung, the gun a Triunic weapon that the centaurs of Taryeanzamh were unable to access until the 18th century. They were superior in one thing however: the use of magic and the institution of the Tempestcallers.

Fleets were sunk by torrential downpours, supply lines broken, lit aflame. The armies that survived were struck by cracking skies and endless thunder, whittled down by glyphs left behind by the shamans that would conjure one natural disaster after the other, all in the attempt to stop the tide of Triunic settlers to the region.
This is the conflict that would define the 17th century in the eastern Forbidden Plains.

player_overview.avoid_if: Avoid it if you do not want to protect a key ruler, or prefer a stable economy and a bright heroic story.
player_overview.how_it_plays: Secure the country and build magical capacity early, infiltrate and conquer the Ogre Valley in mid-campaign, then use lichdom and a necromantic army to support Centaur expansion.
player_overview.overview: The Black Herd begins as the exiled remnants of a Ghanzamh Centaur clan. Beldelk II must recover Markhentakruan, invade the Ogre Valley again, and wager between a short mortal life and lichdom. War, magical research, the seizure of knowledge and the integration of Ogre mages combine into a dark, high-pressure campaign of revival. It leaves little room for distraction.
player_overview.recommended_for: Players who enjoy intensive magical research, a lichdom route, war-crime narratives and a high-pressure campaign of revival.
signature_features: A corpse-explosion spell turns battle casualties into magical progress.
Beldelk's transformation into a lich is the central wager on the country's continuity.
The Ogre Valley combines revenge, knowledge and a route to integrating mages.
player_overview.tagline: Let the exiled Centaurs rebuild the Black Herd through lost magic, necromantic armies and an immortal ruler.

reasons: Lost magic and lichdom create an unusually strong national theme.
Battle casualties, magical projects and the ruler's lifespan are directly connected.
The Ogre Valley offers branches involving revenge, knowledge and integration.
warnings: The death of the key ruler can interrupt long-term magical projects; generic formables are not an unconditional continuation of the Black Herd's unique missions.

positive_indicators: Recovering the knowledge and political continuity of an exiled people.
A route exists for accepting Ogre mages.
Postwar integration is not wholly equivalent to extermination.
values.rationale: The four dimensions, weighted 35/25/25/15, produce 24. Deductions rest on explicit harm to people and knowledge: Beldelk describes his wife as a suitable sacrifice; after conquering Maghargma, his army is allowed to terrorise survivors and seize useful records before burning the rest. Tearbloom records past dissections and a proposal to give surviving spellcasters positions of rank, but does not establish live experimentation or coerced research, so no deduction is made on that basis. The tens of thousands sacrificed and reanimated in Study belong to the Glutton King of the past, not I55. Corpse explosions, necromantic armies and lichdom are not themselves treated as violations of personhood; nor are conquest, Centaur identity, tribal government or central authority. Bands: 0–32 Evil, 33–67 Neutral and 68–100 Good.
red_flags: Explicitly treating his wife as an available sacrifice.
The army terrorises Maghargma's surviving population.
Useful records are seized and the rest of the archives burned.
Ordinary Ogres are disparaged as useless to the operation at Kaent.
